svg.title: The SQLAlchemy stack: seven layers from a Python object down to a row, and what each one hands to the layer below
svg.desc: A static architecture diagram of the layers between a domain object and a database row: your domain objects, the declarative models that map them, the Session that acts as a unit of work with an identity map, Core's expression language, the Engine and its connection pool, the DBAPI driver, and the database itself. Each layer states what it is responsible for and what it hands down. A return path on the right shows rows travelling back up to become objects registered in the identity map. Two callouts mark that Core and the ORM are separable layers and that echo equals True taps the boundary between Core and the Engine.
svg.text: What sits between a Python object and a row in a table
Each layer names what it is responsible for, and what it hands to the layer below. Nothing here is skipped at runtime.
1 · Your domain objects
ada = Member(name="Ada Okonkwo")
Plain Python. Knows nothing about SQL, and should not.
hands down: an object with
attributes set, and no identity yet
2 · Declarative models — the mapping itself
class Member(Base): id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(...)
Which class is which table, which attribute is which column,
and which attribute is a relationship rather than a column.
hands down: a mapped class
plus one shared MetaData holding
every Table it described
3 · The Session — a unit of work
Identity map: one object per primary key, per session.
Tracks pending (added), dirty (changed) and deleted objects.
Decides WHEN work happens: autoflush before a query, flush
on demand, and a commit that ends the transaction.
hands down: an ORDERED batch of
INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, sorted
so foreign keys resolve — plus the
SELECTs your queries asked for
4 · Core — the SQL expression language
select(Book.title).where(Book.copies >= 3)
Table, MetaData, select(), insert(), update(). Compiles an
expression tree into SQL for one dialect, with the values
pulled out as bound parameters rather than pasted in.
hands down: SQL text with ? or
%s placeholders, and a separate
tuple of parameter values
5 · Engine and connection pool
Holds open connections so each unit of work does not pay to
open one. Owns the dialect that decided the SQL above.
hands down: one checked-out
DBAPI connection and its cursor
6 · DBAPI driver — cursor.execute() / executemany()
hands down: the statement, at last
7 · The database — rows, and only rows
rows come back up
Core turns them into tuples; the Session turns those into
objects — and checks the identity map FIRST, so a row you
already hold returns the object you already have.
the ORM
Core
Two layers, and the order matters
Core is a complete library on its own: you can use
select() and insert() with no models and no Session.
The ORM cannot exist without Core, because it emits
its work AS Core expressions. Dropping down is normal.
echo=True taps here
create_engine(url, echo=True) prints every statement
at layer 5, with its parameters. It is the best learning
tool the library has — and a data leak in production.
